Casey Theorem

GeometryCirclesConstructions
Game: Drag four small circles around a big one and watch the straight lines that just touch two circles at once.
How to play: Drag A, B, C or D with a mouse or finger, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Check the identity to see whether the two sides match.
Look for the math

Four circles sit around a bigger circle, each just touching it. Draw the straight lines that just touch two circles at a time. Multiply two pairs of those lengths, add them, and you get the product of the remaining pair. Drag the circles and the sums still match.

From Ptolemy to Casey

For four points A, B, C, D on one circle, Ptolemy's theorem says AB·CD + AD·BC = AC·BD. Casey's theorem replaces the four points by four circles touching a fifth circle: their common tangents take the place of the chords. In the page's numbering the claim is

t12·t34 + t14·t23 = t13·t24.

Letting all four radii shrink to 0 puts the four centres on the big circle and gives Ptolemy back. The applet starts essentially there: its second point is displaced by 0.1 of a pixel, so one radius is about 0.087 instead of exactly 0. That harmless quirk is kept here.

How long is a common tangent?

Put S at the centre of the big circle, of radius R. Circle i has centre P_i at distance d_i from S, so the applet gives it radius |d_i − R|. Give it the signed radius ρ_i = d_i − R: positive outside the big circle, negative inside. The straight piece of a common tangent between circles i and j then has length

t(ij) = √(|P_iP_j|² − (ρ_i − ρ_j)²).

When both circles lie on the same side of the big circle this is the outer tangent (drawn purple here, red in the applet); when one is inside and one outside it is the inner tangent (dashed red here, blue in the applet). The logic test builds both kinds the hard way — from the applet's own circle intersection and homothety construction — and compares them with this formula on hundreds of arrangements.

Why the two products agree

Write each centre in polar form around S, with angle θ_i. The law of cosines turns the formula above into t(ij) = 2·√(d_i·d_j)·|sin((θ_i − θ_j)/2)|: each tangent length is a chord of the unit circle scaled by √(d_i·d_j). Divide Casey's whole equation by √(d_1·d_2·d_3·d_4) and only the four chords remain, so Ptolemy proves Casey at once. This needs the four circles to come in the order A, B, C, D around S; drag one past another and the identity stops holding, which the test checks too.

The radius R cancels from every tangent length, so crossing a circle from inside to outside changes the colours but not the lengths. The applet's page also discusses the converse and whether the circles must be mutually external; this port, like the applet, only shows the identity where the tangents are real.

Try pulling A far outside while leaving B inside: the dashed red tangents cross between the two sides, yet the two products stay equal. Then swap B past D around the circle and press Check to see the identity break.
